ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: 1 of 1 paper appeared to involve live data collection and lacked an ethics approval statement.

table.text: We recruited 234 participants (non-carrier controls n=78, presymptomatic carriers n=115, symptomatic carriers n=41) with CSF, MRI, and clinical (CDR ® + NACC FTLD sum of boxes [CDR-SB]) and executive (Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale-Revised Digit Symbol Substitution Task [DSST] assessments.
table.header: Abstract

table.text: Participants were followed annually for up to 8.6 years (CDR-SB) and 11.5 years (DSST), and linear mixed-effects models were used to estimate individual rates of clinical progression (CDR slope) and executive decline (DSST slope).
table.header: Abstract

table.text: Symptomatic participants were significantly older than presymptomatic carriers and controls and had fewer years of education (p<0.001).
table.formatted: Symptomatic participants were significantly older than presymptomatic carriers and controls and had fewer years of education (p<0.001).
table.header: Participants

table.text: The re-stratified groups based on CDR scores reveal that phenoconverted participants had statistically significantly lower DSST scores (p<0.001) compared with those in the prodromal, asymptomatic, and control groups (Figure 3C).
table.formatted: The re-stratified groups based on CDR scores reveal that phenoconverted participants had statistically significantly lower DSST scores (p<0.001) compared with those in the prodromal, asymptomatic, and control groups (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_9">3C</ref>).
table.header: Carriers in the prodromal window showed a slight elevation of inflammatory proteins and neurodegeneration markers

table.text: To address this, we ran sensitivity analyses re-stratifying our participants by CDR-SB scores, which more sensitively capture granular clinical changes than the simple absence of a formal clinical diagnosis.
table.header: Discussion

ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, but it was not present:

> We recruited 234 participants (non-carrier controls n=78, presymptomatic carriers n=115, symptomatic carriers n=41) with CSF, MRI, and clinical (CDR ® + NACC FTLD sum of boxes [CDR-SB]) and executive (Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale-Revised Digit Symbol Substitution Task [DSST] assessments.

> Participants were followed annually for up to 8.6 years (CDR-SB) and 11.5 years (DSST), and linear mixed-effects models were used to estimate individual rates of clinical progression (CDR slope) and executive decline (DSST slope).

> Symptomatic participants were significantly older than presymptomatic carriers and controls and had fewer years of education (p<0.001).

> The re-stratified groups based on CDR scores reveal that phenoconverted participants had statistically significantly lower DSST scores (p<0.001) compared with those in the prodromal, asymptomatic, and control groups (Figure 3C).

> To address this, we ran sensitivity analyses re-stratifying our participants by CDR-SB scores, which more sensitively capture granular clinical changes than the simple absence of a formal clinical diagnosis.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

The omnibus interaction term between protein-CV scores and disease group in the parametric model with CDR-SB-slopes was statistically significant (F(2,192)=5.59, p=0.004), Ref group: controls), concordant with the bootstrapped model, where the interaction terms were associated with CDR-SB-slopes in symptomatic carriers ( =0.24, CI:[0.02,0.46], Figure 2B-right), but not for presymptomatic carriers ( =0.03, CI:[-0.01, 0.14]), or controls ( = 0.03, CI:[-0.04, 0.09]).

In contrast, the omnibus interaction term between MRI-CV scores and disease group onto CDR-SB-slopes in the parametric model was statistically significant (F(2,192)=3.87, p=0.02, Ref group: controls).

The omnibus three-way interaction term in the parametric model was not associated (F(2,189)=0.13, p=0.86) with CDR-SB-slopes in concordance with the bootstrapped model (Ref group: controls =-0.005, CI:[-0.05,0.05]; presymptomatic carriers = 0.007, CI:[-0.07,0.09]; symptomatic carriers ( =-0.032, CI:[-0.35,0.20]).

Both CSF inflammatory proteins and fronto-insular atrophy are associated with worse executive function cross-sectionally The omnibus interaction term between protein-CV scores and disease group in the parametric model was statistically significant (F(2,217)=4.19, p=0.02) with DSST scores.
Furthermore, the omnibus interaction term between MRI-CV scores and disease group in the parametric model was statistically (F(2,217)=3.12, p=0.04) associated with DSST scores.

The omnibus three-way interaction term in the parametric model was not (F(2,215)=2.03, p=0.13) associated with DSST scores, which is in concordance with the bootstrapped model showing no association with DSST scores (Ref group: controls =-3.73, CI: [-10.32,5.02]; presymptomatic carriers =2.33, CI:[-1.90,7.56]; symptomatic carriers =5.68, CI:[-0.37,12.38]).

Contrary, the omnibus interaction term between protein-CV scores and disease group in the parametric model was not (F(2,217)=0.56, p=0.57) associated with DSST-slope, which is in concordance with the bootstrapped model, where the interaction terms were not associated with DSST slopes (Ref group: controls ( =-0.16, CI:[-0.41,0.13]; presymptomatic carriers ( =-0.11, CI:[-0.54,0.15]); symptomatic carriers ( =0.07, CI:[-0.29,0.43], Figure 2D-right).
The omnibus interaction term between MRI-CV scores and disease group in the parametric model was not (F(2,221)=2.06, p=0.12) associated with DSST-slopes.

The omnibus three-way interaction term in the parametric model was not (F(2,215)=1.04, p=0.35) associated with DSST-slope (Ref group: controls =0.16, CI:[-0.14,0.38]; presymptomatic carriers =-0.26, CI:[-0.70,0.10]; symptomatic carriers =-0.09, CI:[-0.50,0.31]).

table.header: The atrophy-related CSF inflammation pattern is clinically relevant
table.expanded: PCA applied directly to proteomic values in controls and presymptomatic carriers identified one PC that met the abovementioned criteria (explained 37.4% variance), whose scores did not differ significantly between groups (p=0.61), indicating that the proteomic profile of presymptomatic carriers is not distinguishable from that of controls (supplementary material Figure 4B).

table.formatted: Furthermore, the loading structures from two PCAs (residualised within symptomatic carriers and unresidualised in presymptomatic carriers /controls) were statistically significantly correlated (r=0.90, p<0.001) (supplementary material Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_10">4A</ref>), indicating that the residualised PCA within symptomatic carriers reflects a clinical-group-independent covariation structure shared across the remaining cohort, which is distinct from the clinically relevant signal captured in the rCCA.

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = c("p>0.05", "p<0.01", "p>0.05", "p<0.01", 
"p<0.03"), Text = c("Presymptomatic carriers and controls did not differ (p>0.05).", 
"Age and sex were significant covariates (p<0.01).", "The ANCOVA on the MRI-CV scores identified a similar pattern between groups (F(2,229)=22.92, p<0.001) (Figure 1D), showing that MRI-CV scores in symptomatic carriers were significantly higher than in controls (p<0.001) and presymptomatic carriers (p<0.001), but presymptomatic carriers and controls groups did not differ (p>0.05), with age and sex as significant covariates (p<0.01).", 
"The ANCOVA on the MRI-CV scores identified a similar pattern between groups (F(2,229)=22.92, p<0.001) (Figure 1D), showing that MRI-CV scores in symptomatic carriers were significantly higher than in controls (p<0.001) and presymptomatic carriers (p<0.001), but presymptomatic carriers and controls groups did not differ (p>0.05), with age and sex as significant covariates (p<0.01).", 
"In contrast, CDR-SB-slopes was significantly higher in the prodromal stages (p<0.03, Figure 3F)."
)), row.names = c(NA, -5L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"
))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. :::

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 38 columns across 2 data files.
#### Issues Identified

1 file/column combination has at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(File = "DataExampleStudentMath.csv", Column = "address", Issues = "🔒 Personally Identifying Information — Column name suggests personal information (matched: address)"), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = "data.frame") # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 20, FALSE) ```
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 2 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

reproducibility_check.title: Reproducibility Check
reproducibility_check.summary_text:
-  We assessed AND ran 7 R code files for reproducibility (each in an isolated Docker container).
-  2 of 3 scripts ran without error when executed (4 more are run by another script with `source()`).
-  8 installable dependencies detected.

live_data_statements: We recruited 234 participants (non-carrier controls n=78, presymptomatic carriers n=115, symptomatic carriers n=41) with CSF, MRI, and clinical (CDR ® + NACC FTLD sum of boxes [CDR-SB]) and executive (Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale-Revised Digit Symbol Substitution Task [DSST] assessments.

Participants were followed annually for up to 8.6 years (CDR-SB) and 11.5 years (DSST), and linear mixed-effects models were used to estimate individual rates of clinical progression (CDR slope) and executive decline (DSST slope).
Symptomatic participants were significantly older than presymptomatic carriers and controls and had fewer years of education (p<0.001).

The re-stratified groups based on CDR scores reveal that phenoconverted participants had statistically significantly lower DSST scores (p<0.001) compared with those in the prodromal, asymptomatic, and control groups (Figure 3C).

To address this, we ran sensitivity analyses re-stratifying our participants by CDR-SB scores, which more sensitively capture granular clinical changes than the simple absence of a formal clinical diagnosis.

report: This module assesses whether the paper's code could be run on its data, and — because `execute = TRUE` — **actually ran it**. We examined 7 R code files.
#### Run order
The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first), `source()` calls, and numeric filename prefixes.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(Order = 1:7, File = c("rankBasedCommonFunctions.R", 
"rankSumSampler.R", "signRankSampler.R", "LatentNormalTTestSimulationStudy.R", 
"spearmanSampler.R", "ExampleAnalyses.R", "LatentNormalSpearmanSimulationStudy.R"
), "Runs after" = c("—", "—", "—", "signRankSampler.R, rankSumSampler.R", 
"—", "rankBasedCommonFunctions.R, rankSumSampler.R, signRankSampler.R, spearmanSampler.R", 
"spearmanSampler.R"), Basis = c("none", "none", "none", "dependency", 
"none", "dependency", "dependency")), row.names = c(NA, -7L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
#### File paths

Every data path in the code works in the repository as deposited. **2 data paths were built at runtime** with `sprintf()`/`paste()`/`file.path()` instead of written as a literal path — this is fragile authoring practice (it silently breaks if the code is run from a different working directory than the author's own). We resolved all of these on a best-effort basis.
#### Files not run on their own
4 files only define functions, so running them on their own says nothing: a function counts when a script uses it. These files are not counted as scripts. 0 are used by no script in the deposit.

```{r}

# table data --------------------------------------

"rankSumSampler.R", "rankBasedCommonFunctions.R"), "Used by" = c("LatentNormalSpearmanSimulationStudy.R, ExampleAnalyses.R", 
"LatentNormalTTestSimulationStudy.R, ExampleAnalyses.R", "LatentNormalTTestSimulationStudy.R, ExampleAnalyses.R", 
"spearmanSampler.R, signRankSampler.R, rankSumSampler.R, ExampleAnalyses.R"
)), row.names = c(NA, -4L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
#### Execution

**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 7 scripts: 2 ran without error, 0 errored, 1 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse, and 4 were run by another script with `source()`. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions.

"signRankSampler.R", "LatentNormalTTestSimulationStudy.R", "spearmanSampler.R", 
"ExampleAnalyses.R", "LatentNormalSpearmanSimulationStudy.R"), 
    Outcome = c("run_by_source", "run_by_source", "run_by_source", 
    "ran_ok", "run_by_source", "timed_out", "ran_ok"), Detail = c("", 
    "", "", "", "", "timeout", ""), "Time (s)" = c(0, 0, 0, 4.3, 
    0, 300.4, 5.1)), row.names = c(NA, -7L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 15, FALSE)
```
**`setwd()` in the code**

**2 scripts call `setwd()`.** This is bad practice: it hardcodes where the code must run (often an absolute path on the author's own machine) and breaks the moment the code is run anywhere else. To run the code we replaced these calls with a statement that does nothing. Any such script that then ran is **reproducible only after ignoring a `setwd()` that should not have been in the code and needs to be fixed**.
Reproducible after removing `setwd()`: LatentNormalTTestSimulationStudy.R, LatentNormalSpearmanSimulationStudy.R.

```{r}

# table data --------------------------------------

"LatentNormalSpearmanSimulationStudy.R"), "setwd() removed" = c(1L, 
1L), "Path(s) it set" = c("~/GoogleDrive/LabFolderJohnny", "~/GoogleDrive/LabFolderJohnny"
)), row.names = c(NA, -2L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
**Run by another script**

4 scripts are run by another script with `source()`, so they were not run on their own: each script runs in a fresh R process, and on their own a sourced script lacks the packages and objects the sourcing script sets up first. Their outcome is part of the sourcing script's outcome.

"ExampleAnalyses.R")), row.names = c("signRankSampler.R", "rankSumSampler.R",

Below is each problem we found, the scripts it affects, and how to fix it. Fix them in the order given: a problem near the top can cause the ones below it. **A script runs longer than our limit of 5 minutes.** - ExampleAnalyses.R State in the README how long each script runs. If some steps take hours, save their results (such as fitted models) to files, add those to the deposit, and let the script read them, so readers can check the rest without waiting. ### Other problems in the files - LatentNormalTTestSimulationStudy.R calls setwd(), which ties the script to a folder on the author's computer. We replaced the call with one that does nothing so the script could run; it should be removed from the script. - LatentNormalSpearmanSimulationStudy.R calls setwd(), which ties the script to a folder on the author's computer. We replaced the call with one that does nothing so the script could run; it should be removed from the script. ### Comparison with the paper We found no statistical tests in the paper to compare with the output of the code.

text.text: Neuroinflammation is increasingly recognised as a key contributor to frontotemporal dementia (FTD) pathophysiology, yet how inflammatory processes relate to neurodegeneration and clinical progression remains poorly defined.

This study aimed to identify a multivariate cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) inflammatory signature covarying with brain atrophy, and to determine its relevance to clinical and cognitive outcomes in genetic FTD.

We recruited 234 participants (non-carrier controls n=78, presymptomatic carriers n=115, symptomatic carriers n=41) with CSF, MRI, and clinical (CDR ® + NACC FTLD sum of boxes [CDR-SB]) and executive (Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale-Revised Digit Symbol Substitution Task [DSST] assessments.
A regularised canonical correlation analysis (rCCA) was used to derive a shared protein-brain covariance axis.

Participants were followed annually for up to 8.6 years (CDR-SB) and 11.5 years (DSST), and linear mixed-effects models were used to estimate individual rates of clinical progression (CDR slope) and executive decline (DSST slope).
The predictive value of the inflammation-and MRI-based profiles for cross-sectional CDR-SB, CDR slope, DSST and DSST slope were tested in linear models.

Due to floor effects and violations of parametric assumptions, Bias-corrected and accelerated (BCa) confidence intervals (CI) and bootstrap CIs (95%, 5000 replicates) were utilised as the primary inferential criterion in the 2 nd -level linear models; effects were considered non-significant if the 95% BCa CI crossed zero.
The rCCA identified a robust inflammation-brain axis (r=0.89, p<0.001), driven by CXCL9, FLT3L, CCL3, and frontotemporal-insular atrophy pattern.
text.formatted: The rCCA identified a robust inflammation-brain axis (r=0.89, p<0.001), driven by CXCL9, FLT3L, CCL3, and frontotemporal-insular atrophy pattern.

text.text: In symptomatic carriers, the MRI canonical variate was associated with CDR-SB (β=3.80, CI: [0.64, 6.20]) at baseline, whereas the inflammatory protein canonical variate was predictive of CDR-SB slope (β=0.24, CI: [0.02, 0.46]).
Whereas both MRI ( = -7.27, CI:[-14.20, -1.00]) and protein ( = -7.83, CI:[-14.00, -2.16]) canonical variates were linked to DSST cross-sectionally, but not longitudinally.
No significant associations were found in pre-symptomatic carriers or non-carrier controls.

A data-driven CSF inflammatory signature, covarying with frontotemporal-insular atrophy, tracks with clinical severity and cognitive impairment in people with genetic FTD, highlighting inflammation as a candidate therapeutic target and progression biomarker in the earliest clinically manifest stages of disease.

Frontotemporal dementia (FTD) encapsulates a heterogeneous group of clinical syndromes linked to neurodegenerative diseases, ranging from pronounced language symptoms (Primary Progressive Aphasia [PPA]) 1 to behavioural changes (behavioural variant FTD [bvFTD]) 2 , and motor problems 3 .
text.formatted: Frontotemporal dementia (FTD) encapsulates a heterogeneous group of clinical syndromes linked to neurodegenerative diseases, ranging from pronounced language symptoms (Primary Progressive Aphasia [PPA]) <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">1</ref> to behavioural changes (behavioural variant FTD [bvFTD]) <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">2</ref> , and motor problems <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">3</ref> .

text.text: Approximately 10-20% of people with FTD carry an autosomal pathogenic mutation 3 that cause the disease, referred to as genetic FTD.
text.formatted: Approximately 10-20% of people with FTD carry an autosomal pathogenic mutation <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">3</ref> that cause the disease, referred to as genetic FTD.

text.text: The most common mutations include the hexanucleotide (GGGGCC) repeat expansion in Chromosome 9 open reading frame 72 (C9orf72) 4 5 , a loss-of-function mutation in progranulin (GRN) causing haploinsufficiency 6 7 , and missense and splice site mutations in the microtubule-associated protein tau (MAPT) 8 .
text.formatted: The most common mutations include the hexanucleotide (GGGGCC) repeat expansion in Chromosome 9 open reading frame 72 (C9orf72) <ref type="bibr">4 5</ref> , a loss-of-function mutation in progranulin (GRN) causing haploinsufficiency <ref type="bibr">6 7</ref> , and missense and splice site mutations in the microtubule-associated protein tau (MAPT) <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">8</ref> .

text.text: C9orf79 and GRN mutations are related to TDP43 pathology, while MAPT mutations are linked to tauopathies 9 .
text.formatted: C9orf79 and GRN mutations are related to TDP43 pathology, while MAPT mutations are linked to tauopathies <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">9</ref> .

text.text: Presymptomatic people carrying these genetic mutations show marked changes that can be detected years prior to symptom onset in imaging 10 11 , cognition and behaviour 10 12 13 14 , or proteomic profiles 15  16.
text.formatted: Presymptomatic people carrying these genetic mutations show marked changes that can be detected years prior to symptom onset in imaging <ref type="bibr">10 11</ref> , cognition and behaviour <ref type="bibr">10 12 13 14</ref> , or proteomic profiles <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">15</ref>  <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">16</ref>.

text.text: Neuroinflammation is now recognised as a central and dynamic component of the pathogenesis of FTD 17 , and is associated with faster clinical decline 18 19 .
text.formatted: Neuroinflammation is now recognised as a central and dynamic component of the pathogenesis of FTD <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">17</ref> , and is associated with faster clinical decline <ref type="bibr">18 19</ref> .

text.text: This disease process reflects a highly coordinated cascade of cellular and molecular events involving central nervous system-resident glia (astrocytes and microglia), peripheral immune cells (including monocytes and lymphocytes), and diverse signalling mediators such as cytokines and chemokines 17 20 21 22 23 .
text.formatted: This disease process reflects a highly coordinated cascade of cellular and molecular events involving central nervous system-resident glia (astrocytes and microglia), peripheral immune cells (including monocytes and lymphocytes), and diverse signalling mediators such as cytokines and chemokines <ref type="bibr">17 20 21 22 23</ref> .

text.text: Dysregulated cytokine secretion is a key feature of FTD, with converging evidence from blood, CSF, and post-mortem brain tissue 24  25 26 23 .
text.formatted: Dysregulated cytokine secretion is a key feature of FTD, with converging evidence from blood, CSF, and post-mortem brain tissue <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">24</ref>  <ref type="bibr">25 26 23</ref> .

text.text: In a retrospective cohort of genetic FTD, Fenoglio et al (2024) 27 showed that several plasma cytokines, including Tumour Necrosis Factor (TNFα) and interleukins (IL-7, IL-15, IL-16, IL-17A) are significantly upregulated in symptomatic MAPT and GRN mutation carriers 27 .
text.formatted: In a retrospective cohort of genetic FTD, Fenoglio et al (2024) <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">27</ref> showed that several plasma cytokines, including Tumour Necrosis Factor (TNFα) and interleukins (IL-7, IL-15, IL-16, IL-17A) are significantly upregulated in symptomatic MAPT and GRN mutation carriers <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">27</ref> .

text.text: Complementing these findings, largescale CSF proteomic studies in genetic FTD have demonstrated that the three most common mutation groups exhibit distinct pathogenic signatures, with immune-related pathways particularly enriched in symptomatic MAPT carriers 28 .
text.formatted: Complementing these findings, largescale CSF proteomic studies in genetic FTD have demonstrated that the three most common mutation groups exhibit distinct pathogenic signatures, with immune-related pathways particularly enriched in symptomatic MAPT carriers <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">28</ref> .

text.text: In sporadic FTD, multiple studies report upregulation of TNFα, interleukins and chemokines in blood and CSF relative to unaffected controls 29 30 .
text.formatted: In sporadic FTD, multiple studies report upregulation of TNFα, interleukins and chemokines in blood and CSF relative to unaffected controls <ref type="bibr">29 30</ref> .

text.text: In sporadic FTD, proinflammatory cytokines in blood have been found to be strongly associated with central inflammation and shorter survival 23 .
text.formatted: In sporadic FTD, proinflammatory cytokines in blood have been found to be strongly associated with central inflammation and shorter survival <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">23</ref> .

text.text: Taken together, there is substantial evidence for dysregulated immune pathways in FTD, but their relationships with clinical trajectories and neurodegeneration remain incompletely understood.

In a large multicentre FTD consortium study of more than 390 participants, Asken and colleagues 31 quantified IL-6, TNFα and YKL-40 in plasma from presymptomatic and symptomatic mutation carriers and healthy controls, directly linking inflammatory markers to disease progression.
text.formatted: In a large multicentre FTD consortium study of more than 390 participants, Asken and colleagues <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">31</ref> quantified IL-6, TNFα and YKL-40 in plasma from presymptomatic and symptomatic mutation carriers and healthy controls, directly linking inflammatory markers to disease progression.

text.text: Higher TNFα levels were associated with faster clinical decline and temporal lobe atrophy, both cross-sectionally and longitudinally, in MAPT carriers, whereas in C9orf72 carriers, elevated TNFα was related to accelerated cognitive and clinical decline without a clear longitudinal atrophy signature.
These genotype-specific associations highlight the need to better characterise how inflammatory protein abundance maps onto patterns of neurodegeneration across the FTD spectrum.
In line with this, Ullgren and colleagues reported that individual immune-related CSF proteins, such as SERPINA3, are associated with brain atrophy and clinical severity in people with FTD 32 .
text.formatted: In line with this, Ullgren and colleagues reported that individual immune-related CSF proteins, such as SERPINA3, are associated with brain atrophy and clinical severity in people with FTD <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">32</ref> .

text.text: However, no study has yet captured the multidimensional structure of immune-associated multi-protein profiles and their covariance with atrophy patterns and clinical changes over time, leaving a critical gap in our understanding of immune-brain coupling in FTD.

Univariate statistical approaches often cannot capture complex links between modalities, and analysing multidimensional patterns allows us to potentially derive clinically relevant therapeutic target(s) even in presymptomatic stages.

In this study, we aimed to identify a data-driven proteomic profile associated with regional atrophy in genetic FTD, using multivariate statistics of CSF and MRI data from the Genetic FTD Initiative (GENFI) study.

We evaluated whether atrophy-related inflammatory signatures are associated with clinical and executive decline, under the hypothesis that greater inflammatory burden would track with faster deterioration.

We also tested whether these inflammation-atrophy-clinical relationships are already detectable in the presymptomatic phase by comparing healthy non-carrier controls with presymptomatic and symptomatic mutation carriers.

From the GENFI (Genetic Frontotemporal dementia Initiative [https://www.genfi.org]) study (data freeze 8) 10 , n=234 participants who underwent CSF sampling and volumetric T1-weighted MRI acquisition at the same visit, as well as standardised GENFI assessments, were included in this study.
text.formatted: From the GENFI (Genetic Frontotemporal dementia Initiative [<ref type="url" target="https://www.genfi.org">https://www.genfi.org</ref>]) study (data freeze 8) <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">10</ref> , n=234 participants who underwent CSF sampling and volumetric T1-weighted MRI acquisition at the same visit, as well as standardised GENFI assessments, were included in this study.

text.text: Specifically, we included n=41 symptomatic carriers (9 with mutation in MAPT, 12 in GRN, and 20 in C9orf72), n=115 presymptomatic (defined as the absence of a formal diagnosis) mutation carriers (23   with mutation in MAPT, 40 in GRN, and 52 in C9orf72), and n=78 family members without mutations (non-carrier control group).

Participants with another significant medical or psychiatric condition that would interfere with their completion of assessments or impair their safety in the study, or participants who were pregnant or had contraindications to MRI, were excluded.
Participants underwent clinical and cognitive assessments at baseline and annually for up to 11.5 years.
To evaluate clinical decline, we utilised the Sum of Boxes score from the CDR+NACC FTLD, as it has been widely used in FTD clinical trials as primary clinical outcome 33 34 .
text.formatted: To evaluate clinical decline, we utilised the Sum of Boxes score from the CDR+NACC FTLD, as it has been widely used in FTD clinical trials as primary clinical outcome <ref type="bibr">33 34</ref> .

text.text: The CDR® +NACC FTLD captures eight domains, which are particularly affected in FTD phenotypes 35 36 35-37 .
text.formatted: The CDR® +NACC FTLD captures eight domains, which are particularly affected in FTD phenotypes <ref type="bibr">35 36 35-37</ref> .

text.text: The CDR® +NACCFTLD (referred to as CDR-SB onwards) ranges from 0-24, where higher scores indicate more severe symptomology 38.
text.formatted: The CDR® +NACCFTLD (referred to as CDR-SB onwards) ranges from 0-24, where higher scores indicate more severe symptomology <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">38</ref>.

text.text: Executive decline was indexed using the Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale-Revised Digit Symbol Substitution Task (DSST) 39 ,ranging from 100 (no executive dysfunction) to 0 (executive dysfunction).
text.formatted: Executive decline was indexed using the Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale-Revised Digit Symbol Substitution Task (DSST) <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">39</ref> ,ranging from 100 (no executive dysfunction) to 0 (executive dysfunction).

text.text: Briefly, T1-weighted volumetric (1.1 mm isotropic resolution) scans were acquired on 3 Tesla scanners (Siemens Trio
CSF samples were collected by lumbar puncture into polypropylene tubes and stored at -80 °C at each site.
CSF proteins were measured using the proprietary Olink® Target 96 platform.
For more details on the processing of the proteomic data, see supplementary methods.
For descriptive statistics, chi-square and analysis of variance tests compared variables between groups.
To investigate the inflammation-brain covariance axis, we applied a two-level approach previously deployed in our studies 41  42  43 12 23 .
text.formatted: To investigate the inflammation-brain covariance axis, we applied a two-level approach previously deployed in our studies <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">41</ref>  <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">42</ref>  <ref type="bibr">43 12 23</ref> .

text.text: In the first step, we applied a regularised Canonical Correlation Analysis (rCCA) in MATLAB with classical bootstrapping (1000 replicates) to ensure solution stability (supplementary methods for more details on rCCA).

In the second step, we imported the canonical variates (CV) and associated loadings from the previous step into R and constructed a linear model with the "lm" function to model MRI-CV using an interaction term between protein-CV and groups (factor with the following levels; controls=0, presymptomatic carriers=1, and symptomatic carriers=2) as the predictor, with age, sex and scanner model as covariates (MRI-CV~Protein-CV*Group+Age+Sex+scanner model).
Next, we tested for group differences in the resulting CV variables from the protein and MRI data and ran an Analysis of Covariance (ANCOVA) controlling for age and sex.

The ANCOVA was implemented as a linear model using the "lm" function, tested with Type III ANOVA from the car package, and post hoc contrasts were computed using the emmeans package with Bonferroni correction.

To estimate longitudinal trajectories, we fitted linear mixed-effects models (lme4 "lmer") to CDR-SB and DSST scores separately, modelling each as a function of years since baseline (MRI/CSF visit) with random intercepts and slopes per participant.
Participant-specific slopes (CDR slope, DSST slope), and cross-sectional scores and slopes were then compared across the three clinical groups using one-way ANOVAs (supplementary Figure 2).
text.formatted: Participant-specific slopes (CDR slope, DSST slope), and cross-sectional scores and slopes were then compared across the three clinical groups using one-way ANOVAs (supplementary Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_8">2</ref>).

text.text: The predictive value of the protein and MRI latent factors (or CVs) on clinical outcomes was tested in linear models using the CDR-SB, CDR-SB-slope, DSST, and DSST-slope as dependent variables, and CV values*group (factor levels: controls=0, presymptomatic carriers=1, symptomatic carriers=2) as an interaction term.
First, we ran separate models with the protein-CV and MRI-CV as single predictors.
Then, we tested the combined predictive values of the two variables in a three-way interaction model (protein-CV*MRI-CV*Group).
Age, sex, years of education and scanner model were entered as covariates, with controls as the reference group.

To directly test whether the association between the canonical variates and outcomes also differed between symptomatic carrier and presymptomatic carrier groups, the group variable was relevelled with presymptomatic carriers as the reference category (factor levels: presymptomatic carrier=0, control=1, symptomatic carriers=2) and the above models were refitted (referred to as "relevelled model").
To isolate the protein-only signal from the atrophy-linked protein profiles (protein-CV), we residualised the 92 proteins.
For more details on residualisation analyses and consequent application of PCA's, see supplementary methods Symptomatic-carrier group-specific analyses.

Within the symptomatic carrier group, we also tested associations between clinical outcomes and both the residualised protein component and the protein-CV using non-parametric Spearman's rank correlations.

Given the smaller sample size of the symptomatic carrier subgroup, we additionally computed one-tailed Bayesian Spearman's correlations (https://osf.io/gny35/), which enable a more robust statistical interpretation by com-puting Bayes Factors (BF).
text.formatted: Given the smaller sample size of the symptomatic carrier subgroup, we additionally computed one-tailed Bayesian Spearman's correlations (<ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/gny35/">https://osf.io/gny35/</ref>), which enable a more robust statistical interpretation by com-puting Bayes Factors (BF).

text.text: These correlations were complemented by linear models including covariates.

To better capture presymptomatic clinical spectrum effects, we re-stratified groups by CDR-SB score rather than diagnosis alone, following previously established criteria for mutation carriers 40 10 36 : asymptomatic (CDR-SB=0, n=78), prodromal (CDR-SB=0.5, n=19), and symptomatic (CDR-SB≥1, n=44).

text.text: Models were re-run substituting disease status with clinical stage (controls=0, asymptomatic=1, prodromal=2, symptomatic=3).

Due to floor effects and violations of parametric assumptions, Bias-corrected and accelerated (BCa) 44 confidence intervals (CI), bootstrap CIs (95%, 5000 replicates) were utilised as the primary inferential criterion in the 2 nd level linear models using the "boot" function from the boot package: effects were considered non-significant if the 95% BCa CI crossed zero.

text.text: For the interpretation of the Bayesian approach, we set a BF≥3 to evaluate the evidence supporting the alternative hypothesis (a correlation) under the Lee and Wagenmakers criteria 45.

Symptomatic participants were significantly older than presymptomatic carriers and controls and had fewer years of education (p<0.001).

text.text: Of the 41 symptomatic carriers, 2.4% had a clinical diagnosis of AD, 4.9 % ALS, 73 % bvFTD, 2.4% CBS, 4.9 % FTD-ALS, and 12 % PPA.
Clinical data were missing for some participants: controls (n=15), presymptomatic carriers (n=7), and symptomatic carriers (n=8) had no CDR-SB score available at the cross-sectional visit.

Consequently, those with missing outcome data have been excluded from the 2 nd -level analysis.
No batch effects were detected (for more details, see supplementary methods).
The rCCA identified a stable pair of positively correlated CVs (r=0.89, p<0.001, Figure 1C).

To further disentangle the inflammation-brain axis at each level across the three groups, we fitted a bootstrapped linear model that included an interaction term with group (MRI-CV~protein-CV*group) including covariates.

Protein-CV was significantly associated with MRI-CV ( =0.54, CI:[0.40,0.67]), while the interaction terms (protein-CV*group) were not statistically significant for presymptomatic carriers ( =0.05, CI:[-0.09,0.19]) nor symptomatic carriers ( =0.09, CI:[-0.09,0.28]).
Age was positively associated with MRI-CV scores ( =0.01, CI:[0.008,0.02]).
The ANCOVA revealed protein-CV scores differed between groups (F(2,229)=41.57, p<0.001) (Figure 1E).

text.text: Taken together, higher protein-CV scores reflect a pattern of elevated inflammatory signalling related to regional brain atrophy, whereas higher MRI-CV scores reflect greater atrophy across the regions that covary most strongly with the inflammatory profile.

text.text: Our study integrates multiplex CSF proteomics and MRI to investigate the relationship between inflammatory and atrophy profiles, and their clinical relevance and predictive value in genetic FTD.
Our data-driven approach identified a robust inflammation-atrophy covariance axis that predicts clinical decline over time in people with symptomatic FTD.
Specifically, the atrophy-related CSF inflammation pattern predicted worse CDR-SB scores over time in symptomatic FTD gene carriers.
Inflammatory markers and fronto-insular atrophy measures differentiated symptomatic from presymptomatic and control participants, but could not separate presymptomatic from control participants.

To further elucidate protein-brain covariance across the presymptomatic continuum, we re-stratified participants by CDR-SB scores, which more sensitively capture granular clinical changes than the simple absence of a formal clinical diagnosis.
When deploying this approach, we found that inflammatory protein and MRI covarying scores trended towards stepwise divergence between the prodromal and asymptomatic stages.
Examining single protein levels of both CXCL9 (the highest loaded protein derived from the rCCA) and NfL, we detected statistically discernible increases in prodromal stages.
For the 2 nd -level analyses, both group stratification strategies yielded convergent interpretations.
However, within the prodromal FTD cohort, associations with executive dysfunction and clinical progression did not reach statistical significance.

Applying a CCA across proteomics and MRI data, we identified an atrophy-related inflammatory profile that was driven by chemokines (CXCL9, CCL3, CCL2 or MCP-1 and CCL25) that are involved in the recruitment of T-cells and Natural Killer cells 46 , monocytes and macrophages 47 , as well as FLT3L, which promotes the development of dendritic, B, and natural killer cells, and MMP10, which is involved in tissue remodelling 48 49 .
text.formatted: Applying a CCA across proteomics and MRI data, we identified an atrophy-related inflammatory profile that was driven by chemokines (CXCL9, CCL3, CCL2 or MCP-1 and CCL25) that are involved in the recruitment of T-cells and Natural Killer cells <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">46</ref> , monocytes and macrophages <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">47</ref> , as well as FLT3L, which promotes the development of dendritic, B, and natural killer cells, and MMP10, which is involved in tissue remodelling <ref type="bibr">48 49</ref> .

text.text: The CCA also identified an atrophy pattern linked with inflammation, which encompassed frontal and temporal regions and the insula, consistent with their central and early involvement in FTD 50 51 10 .
text.formatted: The CCA also identified an atrophy pattern linked with inflammation, which encompassed frontal and temporal regions and the insula, consistent with their central and early involvement in FTD <ref type="bibr">50 51 10</ref> .

text.text: Notably, interpretation of rCCAderived canonical variates differs from other dimensionality reduction techniques such as PCA: rCCA assigns weights to maximise correlation between modalities, rather than reducing dimensionality within each modality independently.

In this context, higher CSF protein-CV scores indicate increased inflammatory signalling asso-ciated with regional brain atrophy, while higher MRI-CV scores reflect more pronounced atrophy in regions that most strongly covary with the inflammatory profile.
The primary advantage of rCCA is that it treats inflammation and neurodegeneration as an integrated system, capturing complex multimodal crosstalk within a unified statistical framework.
The atrophy-related inflammation CSF pattern, led by CXCL9, identified by our datadriven analysis was elevated in symptomatic patients.
Previous studies focusing on single inflammation markers did not find significant increase in CXCL9 levels in blood and CSF of patients with PPA 52 or bvFTD 29 .
text.formatted: Previous studies focusing on single inflammation markers did not find significant increase in CXCL9 levels in blood and CSF of patients with PPA 52 or bvFTD <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">29</ref> .

text.text: Mechanistically, CXCL9 is an IFN-γ inducible chemokine that signals through the CXCR3 receptor 53 54 , a pathway implicated in T-cell recruitment to the CNS and to sites of inflammation 55 , that potentially contributes to neurodegeneration.
text.formatted: Mechanistically, CXCL9 is an IFN-γ inducible chemokine that signals through the CXCR3 receptor <ref type="bibr">53 54</ref> , a pathway implicated in T-cell recruitment to the CNS and to sites of inflammation <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">55</ref> , that potentially contributes to neurodegeneration.

text.text: On the other hand, multiple studies have shown increased levels of MCP-1 in CSF of people with FTD compared with controls 56 21.
text.formatted: On the other hand, multiple studies have shown increased levels of MCP-1 in CSF of people with FTD compared with controls <ref type="bibr">56 21</ref>.

text.text: MCP1 (also known as CCL2) is implicated in the pathogenesis of a range of human diseases 57 .
text.formatted: MCP1 (also known as CCL2) is implicated in the pathogenesis of a range of human diseases <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">57</ref> .

text.text: MCP1 plays an important role in the inflammatory response, acting as a modulator of leukocytes, and its levels have been linked to AD disease severity 58 59.
text.formatted: MCP1 plays an important role in the inflammatory response, acting as a modulator of leukocytes, and its levels have been linked to AD disease severity <ref type="bibr">58 59</ref>.

text.text: MCP1 is a well-established biomarker that captures aspects of the inflammatory response.

Similarly, IL18, which is a pro-inflammatory cytokine involved in a range of inflammatory responses including pyroptosis 60 , has been found to be increased in both blood serum and the superior frontal cortex at postmortem in people with FTD 30.

text.text: Higher CSF levels of IL18 were also detected in fast-progressing ALS with a C9orf72 mutation 61 .
text.formatted: Higher CSF levels of IL18 were also detected in fast-progressing ALS with a C9orf72 mutation <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">61</ref> .

text.text: Several proteins with high loadings onto the protein canonical variate, including MMP10, CCL25, LAP-TGF-β1, OPG, and SIRT2, have received little to no attention in FTD fluid biomarkers research.

The convergence of these novel biomarkers onto the canonical variate implicates extracellular matrix remodelling, immune cell trafficking, and osteoimmune signalling as underexplored pathological processes in FTD pathogenesis, warranting further investigation.
Although TNF-and IL-6 were not among the top-loading CSF proteins in our rCCA, this may reflect cohort, tissue or platform differences rather than a lack of biological relevance.

Previous research has linked increased plasma levels of TNF-and IL-6 to accelerated longitudinal atrophy in the functional and temporal lobes in MAPT mu-tation carriers, while in C9orf72 mutation carriers higher TNF-abundance was associated with faster functional and cognitive deterioration 31 .

text.text: Given that survival provides a more objective quantification of disease progression than certain clinical scales, Malpetti et al ( 2024) 23 implemented a data-driven approach to capture a proinflammatory signature driven primarily by TNF-, TNF-R1, M-CSF, IL-17A, IL-12, IP-10 and IL-6.

text.text: This pro-inflammatory pattern was significantly associated with a higher probability of shorter survival in sporadic FTD, as well as higher levels of brain inflammation 23 .
text.formatted: This pro-inflammatory pattern was significantly associated with a higher probability of shorter survival in sporadic FTD, as well as higher levels of brain inflammation <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">23</ref> .

text.text: Linking peripheral immune signalling to in-vivo molecular brain imaging, utilising the [ 11 C]-PK11195 radiotracer (a proxy measure for neuroinflammation, binding TSPO 62 63 ), previous PET studied showed elevated neuroinflammation in frontotemporal regions of symptomatic carriers of FTD-related gene mutations as compared to controls 64 .

text.text: However, the pattern of increased [ 11 C]-PK11195 signal was heterogeneous within the symptomatic FTD mutation-carrier group, closely matching brain regions that relate to their clinical syndrome; for example, participants with a MAPT mutation with a clinical diagnosis of bvFTD had elevated binding in frontostriatal regions, whereas a participant with PPA exhibited elevated signal in temporal regions.
A single case study has also described elevated [ 11 C]-PK11195 signal in a presymptomatic MAPT carriers, in absence of detectable regional atrophy 65 .
text.formatted: A single case study has also described elevated [ 11 C]-PK11195 signal in a presymptomatic MAPT carriers, in absence of detectable regional atrophy <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">65</ref> .

text.text: However, capturing the complex and intertwined links between inflammatory signalling and localised atrophy patterns requires robust multimodal statistical integration.
Our implemented rCCA model addresses this complexity.
We deployed an rCCA, which is a model that captures shared variances between our two data sets (protein and MRI).
To examine whether a non-brain-related inflammatory pattern is also clinically relevant we residualised our proteins against protein-CV and extracted the residuals.
This effectively removed any variance that is captured within the inflammation-atrophy axis.
Applying a PCA to the extracted residuals we derived an inflammation pattern that was completely decoupled from the atrophy pattern.
Interestingly, this inflammation signature was not linked to any of the clinical outcomes within the symptomatic group.
This suggests that a generalised immune pattern was not sufficient to explain clinical decline in our cohort, whereas the inflammatory protein-brain axis was able to predict clinical decline.
Hence, the shared variance between the protein and MRI data is clinically relevant and intertwined.
However, CXCL9 levels (the most highly loaded protein derived from the rCCA) alone were associated with clinical progression in participants who phenoconverted.
This supplements the findings from Asken et al. (2023) 31 , which identified TNF-and IL6 as clinically relevant inflammatory markers in genetic FTD.
text.formatted: This supplements the findings from Asken et al. (2023) <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">31</ref> , which identified TNF-and IL6 as clinically relevant inflammatory markers in genetic FTD.

text.text: Further research is needed to investigate whether stepwise therapeutic strategies utilising compounds targeting different parts of the immune system could be efficient diseasemodifying interventions in people with FTD.
The inflammation-atrophy axis identified in symptomatic participants has also translational relevance both as a therapeutic target and as a multivariate biomarker component for trial design.
Three top-loading proteins map onto pathways with existing pharmacological tool compounds: MCP1/CCL2, IL-18 and CCL3.
These can be considered in terms of translational and repurposing readiness from other fields into FTD trials.

MCP1 has been implicated in HIV-associated neurocognitive impairment, which affects around 30-50% of people living with HIV. 88 89 In a small single-arm study, the dual CCR2/CCR5 antagonist cenicriviroc was associated with improved cognitive performance and reduced inflammation over 24 weeks, although it has not yet been tested in FTD. 90 The NLRP3 inflammasome-caspase-1 IL18 axis is a key mediator of innate immune activation across multiple diseases and can be targeted via IL-18 neutralisation or NLRP3/caspase-1 inhibition; notably, the oral NLRP3 inhibitor dapansutrile is in Phase 2 testing in early Parkinson's disease (DAPA-PD; NCT07157735) 91 92 93 94 95 .

text.text: CCL3 is a chemotactic cytokine signalling through CCR1/CCR5. 69 Maraviroc, a CCR5 antagonist approved for HIV, has been shown by Festa et al (2023) to rescue autophagic and neurodegenerative phenotypes in mouse models 96 97 and can cross the blood-brain barrier in people with HIV 66 .

text.text: Collectively, these observations suggest that targeting MCP1/CCL2, IL-18 and CCL3 biology may hold therapeutic promise in FTD and related dementias.
Because the atrophy-related inflammatory pattern we identified was transdiagnostic, CSF inflammatory panels are unlikely to offer strong differential-diagnostic value across the FTD continuum.

However, this same transdiagnostic quality suggests an integrated immunotherapeutic strategy may prove beneficial across individual FTD-spectrum diseases, rather than requiring disease-specific approaches.
This is further supported by a growing body of clinical evidence linking inflammatory profiles to structural brain changes and shorter survival.
Several studies have demonstrated early brain changes in genetic FTD occurring within the presymptomatic window 67 14 .
text.formatted: Several studies have demonstrated early brain changes in genetic FTD occurring within the presymptomatic window <ref type="bibr">67 14</ref> .

text.text: However, in the present study, the CCAdefined inflammatory protein component and the inflammation-related atrophy profiles revealed no statistically significant differences between healthy controls and presymptomatic mutation carriers.

This is consistent with De Houwer et al. (2025) 28 , who employed proximity extension assay Olink technology to quantify over 2,900 proteins in CSF samples of people with genetic FTD and similarly identified no differentially abundant proteins between presymptomatic participants and controls.
text.formatted: This is consistent with De Houwer et al. (2025) <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">28</ref> , who employed proximity extension assay Olink technology to quantify over 2,900 proteins in CSF samples of people with genetic FTD and similarly identified no differentially abundant proteins between presymptomatic participants and controls.

text.text: One explanation is that CSF sampling in our cohort occurred early in the disease trajectory, at a point when pathological processes remain below the detection threshold of current proteomic tools.
Had samples been collected closer to phenoconversion, differences in both inflammatory proteins and inflammation-related MRI patterns relative to controls would more likely be apparent.

To address this, we ran sensitivity analyses re-stratifying our participants by CDR-SB scores, which more sensitively capture granular clinical changes than the simple absence of a formal clinical diagnosis.
We identified stepwise (although not statistically significant) divergence be- Another aspect to consider is the limitations of the proteomic approach.

Although proximity extension assay technology robustly quantifies a pre-specified set of proteins, the human proteome encompasses tens of thousands of distinct proteins, the majority of which remain unmeasured 68 69 70 .
text.formatted: Although proximity extension assay technology robustly quantifies a pre-specified set of proteins, the human proteome encompasses tens of thousands of distinct proteins, the majority of which remain unmeasured <ref type="bibr">68 69 70</ref> .

text.text: Crucially, this platform requires intact proteins with accessible epitopes for dual-antibody binding, and therefore cannot reliably detect short peptides, protein fragments, or heavily modified proteoformsspecies that may undergo early changes in FTD and carry prognostic or mechanistic significance.
Unbiased, mass spectrometry-based proteomics approaches therefore offer a complementary and potentially more sensitive strategy for biomarker discovery in this context.

In line with this, a recent GENFI study 16 , employing mass spectrometry in CSF of participants with genetic FTD, found that the immune response co-expression module did not significantly differentiate presymptomatic carriers from controls, though other proteomic clusters showed presymptomatic changes, providing further evidence that immune dysregulation may not be detectable in CSF during the presymptomatic phase.
text.formatted: In line with this, a recent GENFI study <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">16</ref> , employing mass spectrometry in CSF of participants with genetic FTD, found that the immune response co-expression module did not significantly differentiate presymptomatic carriers from controls, though other proteomic clusters showed presymptomatic changes, providing further evidence that immune dysregulation may not be detectable in CSF during the presymptomatic phase.

text.text: Given that neither CSF inflammation proteomics nor the CCA-derived profiles detected significant immune dysregulation in presymptomatic carriers, it is possible that neuroinflammatory activation and immunological changes may be spatially restricted to the brain parenchyma at this disease stage and not yet reflected in the CSF compartment.

Future studies incorporating positron emission tomography with translocator protein (TSPO) radioligands could directly visualise microglial-driven neuroinflammation in presymptomatic mutation carriers 71 , offering a more sensitive and spatially resolved window into the temporal dynamics of neuroinflammation in presymptomatic FTD.
text.formatted: Future studies incorporating positron emission tomography with translocator protein (TSPO) radioligands could directly visualise microglial-driven neuroinflammation in presymptomatic mutation carriers <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">71</ref> , offering a more sensitive and spatially resolved window into the temporal dynamics of neuroinflammation in presymptomatic FTD.

text.text: Several limitations of this study should be considered when interpreting our findings.

First, whilst the Olink Target 96 Inflammation platform is scalable and widely accessible, it quantifies 92 pre-selected inflammatory proteins, but does not capture the whole complexity of inflammatory cascades and other disease-relevant pathways, including synaptic and metabolic changes.
Second, medical history data on past or current infections and inflammatory conditions were not available.
However, our study focussed on a atrophy-related inflammatory protein pattern in CSF, which may reduce capturing signals related to peripheral conditions.
Third, our study was insufficiently powered to investigate group differences in the inflammation-atrophy axis between gene mutation cohorts (C9orf72, GRN, or MAPT).
Pooling the genetic subgroups in the rCCA may mask mutation-specific inflammation-atrophy associations, as previous studies identified mutation-specific differences in protein abundance 28 27 .
text.formatted: Pooling the genetic subgroups in the rCCA may mask mutation-specific inflammation-atrophy associations, as previous studies identified mutation-specific differences in protein abundance <ref type="bibr">28 27</ref> .

text.text: Finally, CSF proteomic data were available cross-sectionally only and the rCCA deployed is a linear statistical model that assumes linear patterns in the protein-brain covariance matrix; hence, non-linear associations are not captured.
This is particularly relevant for inflammation, which is not a static process but rather a highly complex, dynamic mechanism that may change over time.

Future research incorporating longitudinal data is needed to capture non-linear trajectories of inflammatory processes across the pre-symptomatic and symptomatic windows of FTD, as well as multimodal and sensitive approaches that can capture changes in brain versus peripheral inflammation early in FTD, even before symptoms.

In conclusion, our study identified a robust data-driven association between CSF inflammatory proteins and brain atrophy in genetic FTD, that is driven predominantly by older symptomatic participants.

The atrophy-related inflammatory protein pattern identified in this study is clinically relevant, predicting both disease progression and cross-sectional executive dysfunction in symptomatic individuals.
These findings support the use of multivariate approaches to examine complex relationships and dynamics between brain atrophy, inflammation and clinical outcomes in FTD.

Our study provides further evidence that inflammatory pathways are implicated in genetic FTD and related to worse clinical outcomes, representing potential therapeutic targets in this population.    across the clinical continuum for (A) MRI-CV scores, (B) log10-transformed Neurofilament light chain (log10 NfL) levels, (C) longitudinal clinical progression captured by the CDR plus NACC FTLD-SB slope (CDR -slope), (D) protein-CV scores, (E) abundance levels of CXCL9 (the highest loaded protein derived from the Regularised Canonical Correlation Analysis, (F) executive function indexed by the Digit Symbol Substitution Test.

However, the BF=1.07 provides only anecdotal evidence for this correlation (Figure2Eleft).

The omnibus three-way interaction term in the parametric model was not significantly (F(2,189)=0.26, p=0.9) associated with CDR-SB scores in concordance with the bootstrapped model (Ref group: controls ( =-0.08, CI:[-0.42, 0.27]); presymptomatic carriers ( =0.08, CI:[-0.38,0.44]); symptomatic carriers ( =-0.11, CI:[-3.13, 2.97]).

The omnibus interaction term between protein-CV scores and disease group in the parametric model with CDR-SB-slopes was statistically significant (F(2,192)=5.59, p=0.004), Ref group: controls), concordant with the bootstrapped model, where the interaction terms were associated with CDR-SB-slopes in symptomatic carriers ( =0.24, CI:[0.02,0.46], Figure 2B-right), but not for presymptomatic carriers ( =0.03, CI:[-0.01, 0.14]), or controls ( = 0.03, CI:[-0.04, 0.09]).
The relevelled model showed that the association between protein-CV and CDR-SB-slopes was not different between symptomatic and presymptomatic carriers (β=0.18, CI:[-0.04, 0.39].

Refitting the bootstrapped linear model using only data from symptomatic mutation carriers indicated that protein-CV scores were positively associated with CDR-SB-slopes (β=0.23, CI:[0.20,0.45], Rho=0.34, BF=3.28, Figure 2F-left).

In contrast, the omnibus interaction term between MRI-CV scores and disease group onto CDR-SB-slopes in the parametric model was statistically significant (F(2,192)=3.87, p=0.02, Ref group: controls).

However, in the bootstrapped model, the interaction terms were not associated with CDR-SB-slopes (Ref group: controls ( =0.03, CI:[-0.05,0.09]; presymptomatic ( =0.03, CI:[-0.03,0.11]; and symptomatic carriers ( = 0.24, CI:[-0.03,0.53], Figure 2B-left).
The relevelled model showed that the associa-tion between MRI-CV and CDR-SB-slopes did not differ between symptomatic and presymptomatic carriers (β=0.21, CI:[-0.07,0.50]).

The omnibus three-way interaction term in the parametric model was not associated (F(2,189)=0.13, p=0.86) with CDR-SB-slopes in concordance with the bootstrapped model (Ref group: controls =-0.005, CI:[-0.05,0.05]; presymptomatic carriers = 0.007, CI:[-0.07,0.09]; symptomatic carriers ( =-0.032, CI:[-0.35,0.20]).

Both CSF inflammatory proteins and fronto-insular atrophy are associated with worse executive function cross-sectionally The omnibus interaction term between protein-CV scores and disease group in the parametric model was statistically significant (F(2,217)=4.19, p=0.02) with DSST scores.

This is concordant with the bootstrapped model where the interaction term in symptomatic carriers is linked with DSST scores ( =-7.83, CI:[-14.00,-2.16], Figure 2C-right) but not for the presymptomatic carriers ( =-1.80, CI:[-6.07,2.33]) nor controls ( =1.51, CI:[-2.70,5.63]).
The relevelled model showed no association between protein-CV and DSST scores between symptomatic and presymptomatic carriers (β=-5.2, CI:[-10.97,0.10]).

Refitting the bootstrapped linear model using only data from symptomatic mutation carriers indicated that protein-CV scores were associated with worse DSST scores (β=-6.09, CI:[-11.56,-2.19], Rho=-0.40, BF=44.4, Figure 2G-left).
Furthermore, the omnibus interaction term between MRI-CV scores and disease group in the parametric model was statistically (F(2,217)=3.12, p=0.04) associated with DSST scores.

This is concordant with the bootstrapped model showing that MRI-CV scores were statistically associated with DSST scores in symptomatic carriers ( =-7.27, CI:[-14.20,-1.00], Figure 2C-left) but not for presymptomatic carriers ( =-1.07, CI:[-5.40,3.28]) nor controls ( =0.54, CI:[-4.09,4.78]).
The relevelled model showed that the association between MRI-CV and DSST was not different between symptomatic and presymptomatic carriers (β=-5.20, CI:[-11.63,0.49]).

The omnibus three-way interaction term in the parametric model was not (F(2,215)=2.03, p=0.13) associated with DSST scores, which is in concordance with the bootstrapped model showing no association with DSST scores (Ref group: controls =-3.73, CI: [-10.32,5.02]; presymptomatic carriers =2.33, CI:[-1.90,7.56]; symptomatic carriers =5.68, CI:[-0.37,12.38]).

Contrary, the omnibus interaction term between protein-CV scores and disease group in the parametric model was not (F(2,217)=0.56, p=0.57) associated with DSST-slope, which is in concordance with the bootstrapped model, where the interaction terms were not associated with DSST slopes (Ref group: controls ( =-0.16, CI:[-0.41,0.13]; presymptomatic carriers ( =-0.11, CI:[-0.54,0.15]); symptomatic carriers ( =0.07, CI:[-0.29,0.43], Figure 2D-right).
The relevelled model indicated that the association between protein-CV and DSST-slopes was not different between symptomatic carriers and presymptomatic carriers (β=0.18, CI:[-0.14,0.57]).

Refitting the bootstrapped linear model using only data from symptomatic mutation carriers indicated that protein-CV scores were not associated with DSST-slope (β=-0.16, CI:[-0.45,0.14], Rho=-0.12, BF=0.74, Figure 2H-left).
The omnibus interaction term between MRI-CV scores and disease group in the parametric model was not (F(2,221)=2.06, p=0.12) associated with DSST-slopes.

In concordance with the bootstrapped model showing that the interactions were not associated with DSSTslopes (Ref group: controls =-0.15, CI:[-0.42,0.13]; presymptomatic carriers =-0.21, CI:[-0.69,0.11]; symptomatic carriers =0.20, CI:[-0.19,0.57], Figure 2D-left).
The relevelled model showed that the association between MRI-CV and DSST slopes was statistically different between symptomatic and presymptomatic carriers (β=0.41, CI:[0.06,0.84]).

The omnibus three-way interaction term in the parametric model was not (F(2,215)=1.04, p=0.35) associated with DSST-slope (Ref group: controls =0.16, CI:[-0.14,0.38]; presymptomatic carriers =-0.26, CI:[-0.70,0.10]; symptomatic carriers =-0.09, CI:[-0.50,0.31]).

Figure 1: Regularised Canonical Correlation Analysis (rCCA) of CSF inflammatory proteins and MRI regional values.
(A)Brain plot showing contribution loadings for MRI regional values (representative slice; for a full overview of regional loadings, refer to Supplementary Material 1).
Brain regions of interest included the dorsolateral prefrontal (DLPFC), ventromedial prefrontal (VMPFC), orbitofrontal (OF), and motor (MOT) regions.
The temporal lobe was subdivided into medial temporal (MT), lateral temporal (LT), temporal pole (TP), and supratemporal areas.
The posterior cortical regions were subdivided into sensory (S), medial parietal (MP), lateral parietal (LP), and occipital (OCC).
(B) Syndromic plot displaying the ten highest-loading CSF proteins contributing to the protein canonical variate (Protein-CV).

(C) Positive correlation between MRI-derived (y-axis; MRI-CV) and CSF-derived (x-axis; Protein-CV) rCCA participant scores, coloured by disease status (HC = healthy controls [blue], PMC = presymptomatic mutation carriers [mint green], SMC = symptomatic mutation carriers [Vermilion]); the dashed line represents the overall linear model, and marginal plots display density distributions per group.
(D) Violin plots of MRIderived CCA participant scores (MRI-CV) by disease status.
(E) Violin plots of CSFderived rCCA participant scores (Protein-CV) by disease status.
Individual datapoints are not plotted to prevent disclosure of genetic status.
Figure 2: CSF inflammatory protein and MRI canonical variates by clinical and cognitive progression.
(A, E) Cross-sectional associations with clinical severity (CDR plus NACC FTLD-SB): (A) Primary analysis mapping baseline clinical severity against (left) MRI-CV and (right) Protein-CV scores.
(E) Sensitivity validation comparing (left) Protein-CV scores against (right) residualised protein PC1 scores.
(B, F) Longitudinal analyses of clinical progression (CDR plus NACC FTLD-SB slope): (B) Primary analysis mapping participant trajectories against (left) MRI-CV and (right) Protein-CV scores.
(F) Sensitivity validation comparing (left) Protein-CV scores against (right) residualised protein PC1 scores.

(C, G) Cross-sectional associations with executive functioning (Digit Symbol Substitution Test): (C) Primary analysis mapping baseline executive function against (left) MRI-CV and (right) Protein-CV scores.
(G) Sensitivity validation comparing (left) Protein-CV scores against (right) residualised protein PC1 scores.
(D, H) Longitudinal analyses of executive deterioration (DSST slope): (D) Primary analysis mapping longitudinal rates of cognitive change against (left) MRI-CV and (right) Protein-CV scores.
(H) Sensitivity validation comparing (left) Protein-CV scores against (right) residualised protein PC1 scores.
Individual datapoints are not plotted to prevent disclosure of genetic status.

For all panels, linear regressions map associations with regression coefficients and 95% bias-corrected and accelerated confidence intervals (95% BCa CI) reported only for symptomatic mutation carriers.
